hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to high-contrast, compact, dark focal features—typically round or oval shapes such as eyes, noses, circular holes, spheres, or dark animal heads. These features are consistently rendered in deep black or dark charcoal tones and are set against a significantly lighter, monochromatic background of white, light gray, or silver, creating a sharp dark-on-light contrast. The neuron demonstrates invariance to object identity (responding to both biological features like pupils and snouts and inanimate objects like bowling balls or mechanical holes) and surface texture (activating for both glossy, wet surfaces with highlights and matte, void-like shapes). The activating dark feature is generally centered or positioned as the primary visual anchor, typically occupying approximately 10–30% of the image area.
